newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Cohen meets Kuwaiti leader, reviews U.S. troops.
newsitem.headline: Cohen meets Kuwaiti leader, reviews U.S. troops.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen held talks with Kuwait's ruler on Monday and inspected American military armour stationed in the country for any future Gulf conflict.
He met the emir, Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, and other officials and was to hold a news conference before flying to Bahrain on the third leg of a five-nation Gulf visit.

Cohen earlier visited nearby Camp Doha, about 100 km (60 miles) from the Iraqi border, and told U.S. soldiers stationed there that they were "a premier example of power projection" against Iraq and Iran.

Flanked by two big mobile 155mm artillery pieces, the secretary repeated his oft-stated message that the U.S. military would remain in the Gulf as long as Iraq and Iran presented a threat to the world's biggest oil supply.
Hundreds of U.S. M-1A tanks, artillery pieces and armoured personnel carriers are in storage at Camp Doha in case of any new attack on Kuwait from Iraq like the one that prompted the 1991 Gulf War.
"Saddam Hussein is constantly probing any which way that he can find weakness in our force levels," Cohen said of Iraq's president.

"What you are doing here is greatly appreciated by the Kuwaiti people and the American people," he said, referring to Kuwait's enthusiastic support for the U.S. presence after an American-led military coalition drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait in the Gulf War.
About 2,700 U.S. troops and dozens of American fighter jets are stationed in Kuwait on a permanent basis, although the troop figure often rises because of a constant series of military exercises.
The oil-rich state bears the full cost of maintaining the U.S. presence except for troop paychecks and spends $180 million a year on Camp Doha alone.
The camp, surrounded by desert, concrete and barbed-wire walls, maintains a high security posture, especially after a bomb attack in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, last year which killed 19 U.S. airmen.
With the June 25 anniversary of that blast approaching, Cohen reminded the American troops that "this is a very high threat area" for possible attacks.
"You have to remain alert at all times," he said.
Saudi Arabia and the United States are still investigating the Dhahran attack on a military housing complex but have set no blame, including whether it was sponsored by another country.

In a visit to Saudi Arabia on Sunday, Cohen pressed top Saudi officials to provide more information to the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation on its probe into the bombing. The FBI has complained of a lack of cooperation, including alleged reluctance by the Saudis to give access to suspects.
Following the talks in Bahrain, Cohen will also visit the United Arab Emirates and Oman before flying home on Wednesday.
